content.thinking: This intervention explains peer review as a quality-control mechanism, touching on competence, accountability, and openness through a mildly vivid framing of scientific scrutiny. It's fairly dry and expository but does address self-correction concerns, so I'm estimating a moderate trust boost around +2.1, landing in a mid-to-upper range.

parsed_output.reasoning_summary: The peer-review text is a didactic process-transparency message: it explains external quality control by competing experts, required revisions, and rejection rates, which maps almost directly onto the competence, integrity and openness subscales of the multidimensional trust battery (and, via 'independent experts worldwide reach the same conclusions', lightly onto consensus/accountability). Because it addresses the classic skeptic objection that findings are 'just one researcher's opinion,' it should be an above-average but not top arm on trust — it is expository rather than narrative or messenger-based, and ends with a mildly preachy 'trust the process' that can invite slight reactance among the skeptical. I therefore place the primary trust ATE at roughly d≈0.09 (+2.2 points), with the re-asked, pre-anchored single items (trust_post, belief_post) attenuated and distrust falling a bit less in absolute value than trust rises (distrust items are stickier and partly identity-expressive). Downstream outcomes are ordered trust > institutional trust/scientist-role/funding > belief/concern > general and specific policy > behavioral intentions, each shrinking substantially because peer review says nothing about policy instruments or personal action. Incentivized outcomes get near-zero forecasts (a few cents of donation, under one percentage point of newsletter signup), consistent with megastudy evidence that attitude shifts do not translate into costly behavior in one sitting.
